entries.author: cbenz

entries.quote: Indeed I can't see the point of shipping the "AI first" feature as a whole editor. It seems to me that it should be a feature of any editor, or else I'd like to be convinced by arguments less marketing oriented than those I see on the home page.
entries.outcome: Cursor raised $2.3B at a $29.3B valuation and crossed $1B in annualized revenue.
entries.outcomeDetail: Cursor launched in 2023 as a standalone AI-first editor. By November 2025 it had raised $2.3 billion at a $29.3 billion post-money valuation and crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, with millions of developers using it.
entries.note: The 'whole editor' premise was the product, not a feature. Cursor's standalone IDE became the category leader.

entries.author: albert_e
entries.cardQuote: Does this really need to be a separate IDE (that too a fork of VS Code) than being just a VS Code extension? Getting a Rabbit R1 vibe
entries.quote: Does this really need to be a separate IDE (that too a fork of VS Code) than being just a VS Code extension? Getting a Rabbit R1 vibe
entries.outcome: Cursor reached a $29.3B valuation; the Rabbit R1 comparison did not hold.
entries.outcomeDetail: The comment compared Cursor to the Rabbit R1, a standalone AI gadget that flopped. Cursor instead became one of the most valuable AI coding companies, raising $2.3 billion at a $29.3 billion valuation in November 2025.
entries.note: The form-factor worry was reasonable. The comparison to a failing gadget was not; developers paid for the separate IDE at scale.

entries.author: PheonixPharts
entries.cardQuote: anything that only really works 13.86% of the time, when the verification of the work takes nearly as much time as the work would have anyway, isn't useful.
entries.quote: It's worth pointing out that on their eval set for "issues resolved" they are getting 13.86%. While visually this looks impressive compared to the others, anything that only really works 13.86% of the time, when the verification of the work takes nearly as much time as the work would have anyway, isn't useful. The problem with this entire space is that we have VC hype for work that should ultimately still be being done in research labs. Nearly all LLM results are completely mind blowing from a research perspective but still a long way from production ready for all but a small subset of problems. The frustrating thing, as someone working in this space awhile, is that VCs want to see game changing products ship overnight. Teams working on the product facing end of these things are all being pushed insanely hard to ship. Most of those teams are solving problems never solved before, but given deadlines as though they are shipping CRUD web apps. The kicker is that despite many teams doing all of this, because the technology still isn't there, they still disappoint "leadership". I've personally seen teams working nights and weekends, implementing solutions to never before seen problems in a few weeks, and still getting a thumbs down when they cross the finish line. To really solve novel problems with LLMs will take a large amount of research, experimentation and prototyping of ideas, but people funding this hype have no patience for that. I fear we'll get hit by a major AI winter when investors get bored, but we'll end up leaving a lot of value on the table simply because there wasn't enough focus and patience on making these incredible tools work.
entries.outcome: Cognition raised $2B at a $48B valuation; Devin run-rate revenue neared $900M.
entries.outcomeDetail: Devin's 13.86% resolve rate was real at launch, but Cognition kept improving the agent and sold it to Nvidia, Citi, GE Aerospace, and Mercedes-Benz. By September 2026 Cognition had raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation and reported nearly $900 million in run-rate revenue.
entries.note: The benchmark critique was sharp and correct at the time. The mistake was treating an early eval as a permanent ceiling.

entries.author: realusername
entries.cardQuote: Good code generation with a UI is already a thing since the 90s, it's replacing developers as much as Frontpage and WordPress do.
entries.quote: It's the AI hype group which are in a stage of denial. "Surely if we generate code, it means we can replace developers right?" Well no, it's not nearly enough. Good code generation with a UI is already a thing since the 90s, it's replacing developers as much as Frontpage and WordPress do. The average developer writes 100 lines per day anyways so the speed of writing those lines doesn't matter. Software is an interpersonal job at core and the most precise definition of a business. The day software engineers are replaced by a machine, there's no job for the CEO itself honestly and that's also why this job is well paid. I'm sure it will be all over LinkedIn though, despite this paradox. Those new tools will be there in the background but cannot replace a software engineer.
entries.outcome: Cognition reached a $48B valuation and nearly $900M in run-rate revenue on Devin.
entries.outcomeDetail: The comment said code generation with a UI could not replace developers, comparing it to Frontpage and WordPress. Devin did not replace developers, but it became a large enterprise product, and Cognition was valued at $48 billion in September 2026.
entries.note: The analogy underestimated how much paid work an agent could absorb even without replacing engineers outright.

entries.author: latexr
entries.cardQuote: The current crop of AI is cool for coding demos, not for solving real relevant problems.
entries.quote: > I'm probably dumb as hell, because I just can't get it to do anything remotely useful Rather, your “problem” is that you’re likely not writing uninteresting cookie cutter boilerplate that everyone can do and has done hundreds of times. The current crop of AI is cool for coding demos, not for solving real relevant problems. > Just give me a product that works as advertised and I'll throw money your way The people hyping this crap only care about the second part of that sentence. The first one is an afterthought.
entries.outcome: Devin moved from demos to enterprise customers and a $48B parent valuation.
entries.outcomeDetail: Devin's early demos drew skepticism, but Cognition turned it into an agent used for chip design at Nvidia, aviation at GE Aerospace, and financial services at Citi. Cognition raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation in September 2026.
entries.note: The line between 'coding demos' and 'real relevant problems' moved further than the comment expected.

entries.author: ipsum2
entries.cardQuote: It's not hard to make, its a relatively simple CLI tool so there's no moat. Also, the minified source code is available.
entries.quote: It's not hard to make, its a relatively simple CLI tool so there's no moat. Also, the minified source code is available.
entries.outcome: Claude Code reached a $2.5B+ annualized run rate by February 2026.
entries.outcomeDetail: Anthropic launched Claude Code as a research preview in February 2025. By February 2026 Anthropic said Claude Code's run-rate revenue had passed $2.5 billion, enterprise customers were over half of it, and Claude Code was authoring an estimated 4% of public GitHub commits.
entries.note: A CLI can be easy to clone and still hard to make trusted at scale. The moat was the model, harness, and distribution, not the terminal UI.

entries.author: dimal
entries.cardQuote: LLMs are terrible at it when it’s slightly non-obvious and since everyone is focusing on vibe coding, I doubt they’ll get any better.
entries.quote: Bugs? Those are grubby human work. Seriously, everyone should get good at fixing bugs. LLMs are terrible at it when it’s slightly non-obvious and since everyone is focusing on vibe coding, I doubt they’ll get any better.
entries.outcome: Codex improved rapidly and passed 5 million weekly active users by June 2026.
entries.outcomeDetail: OpenAI shipped successive Codex models and a desktop app. By June 2026 OpenAI said Codex had more than 5 million weekly active users and that usage inside businesses had grown sixfold since January.
entries.note: The prediction that LLMs would not get better at non-obvious bugs was the wrong half of the critique. Bug-fixing improved substantially.

entries.author: CSMastermind
entries.cardQuote: If you just let it run loose on a codebase without close supervision you'll devolve into a mess of technical debt pretty quickly.
entries.quote: In my testing with it anything that requires a bit of critical thought gets completely lost. It's about on par with a bad junior engineer at this point. For instance I ask it to make a change and as part of the output it makes a bunch of value on the class nullable to get rid of compiler warnings. This technically "works" in the sense that it made the change I asked for and the code compiles but it's clearly incorrect in the sense that we've lost data integrity. And there's a bunch of other examples like that I could give. If you just let it run loose on a codebase without close supervision you'll devolve into a mess of technical debt pretty quickly.
entries.outcome: Codex improved beyond the 'bad junior engineer' stage and reached enterprise scale.
entries.outcomeDetail: The comment described an early Codex version that lost the thread on changes requiring judgment. OpenAI kept shipping updates, and by 2026 Codex had millions of weekly users, including a fast-growing share of knowledge workers.
entries.note: The technical-debt warning was fair. The implied ceiling was not.

entries.author: s__s
entries.cardQuote: I just don’t think it’s ever going to be practical to write and maintain software (front or backend) using conversational text prompts.
entries.quote: I’m not convinced of that yet. Visual UI builders have been a thing for decades and this is more or less the same thing except the input mechanism has changed. Instead of point and click you’re prompting it with text. I think there are a lot of problems, but mainly I just don’t think it’s ever going to be practical to write and maintain software (front or backend) using conversational text prompts. It’s a very imprecise tool for the job.
entries.storyTitle: v0: Generate UI with simple text prompts
entries.outcome: v0 passed 3.5M users; Vercel raised at a $9.3B valuation.
entries.outcomeDetail: Vercel launched v0 in 2023 as a text-to-UI generator. By September 2025 v0 had more than 3.5 million unique users, Teams and Enterprise were over half of its revenue, and Vercel raised a $300 million Series F at a $9.3 billion valuation.
entries.note: The critique of prompt imprecision was fair. The prediction that conversational building would never be practical was not; v0 became a mass-market front door for Vercel.

entries.author: ShamelessC
entries.cardQuote: How exactly does a company of 12 people implementing the research of others on compute paid for by investors lacking in technical savvy “change everything”?
entries.quote: How exactly does a company of 12 people implementing the research of others on compute paid for by investors lacking in technical savvy “change everything”? Is it really possible to just pay for an article in rolling stone now? You could write essentially the exact same piece about dozens of other start ups in the generative AI space right now. Might be effective PR, but it’s bad advertising.
entries.outcome: Suno raised $400M+ at a $5.4B valuation and reported $300M+ in revenue.
entries.outcomeDetail: Suno launched publicly in 2024 with a small team and a Rolling Stone profile. By June 2026 it had raised more than $400 million in Series D at a $5.4 billion valuation, and its CEO said it was far beyond 2 million paid subscribers and $300 million in revenue.
entries.note: The '12 people implementing research' framing underestimated the product and distribution. Suno became the defining consumer AI music app.

entries.author: anigbrowl
entries.cardQuote: Likely takeup by musicians: close to zero, although a few singers will use it for ready-made songs/backing tracks
entries.quote: Good for: wallpaper music for stores, youtubers, other library music consumers Likely takeup by musicians: close to zero, although a few singers will use it for ready-made songs/backing tracks that they can warble over, and a very few of those will be good or distinctive as singers. The songs themselves won't stick because the output won't be copyrightable; talented singers will learn to write their own songs or get partnered with people who have a track record in the relevant genre. All of these music AI products miss the mark because they generate mixes, instead of stems or MIDI. There's already a superfluity of music; nobody wants an infinity jukebox full of songs they don't know and have to learn. While the technical achievement is very impressive, it's notable that none of the founders in this story identify as musicians or exhibit any idea how to cater to them. Fully AI (including vocal synthesis) may have a few individual breakouts but will be limited by two factors. One, most people using such tools will want something easy rather than challenging, so there will be more and more lowest-common-denominator dreck - already a problem in human-generated music. And I'm sorry, but that's what Suno churns out. I tried half a dozen prompts on a few different genres that I used to DJ and the results where all instant needle skips. I hope v3 lets you specify instrumental/no vocal because v2 just ignores that and churns out vapid filler. It's very technically impressive, I don't want to claim otherwise. But it's also utterly uninteresting. Two, live performances won't be possible, and the world only has room for so many novelty acts like Hatsune Miku. The biggest market for virtual singers will be kids under 10 who want easily digestible music and don't value assortativity, but don't have much discretionary spending power and won't spend big on childhood nostalgia later. Edit (based partly on others' comments): while I think this sort of tool is bad for creating interesting music, it's a fantastic core model for a game of Record Label Simulator where you play the person that writes big checks and you try to wheel and deal your stable of eager young talent to the top of the charts.
entries.outcome: Suno signed licensing deals with Warner Music and BMG and launched licensed models.
entries.outcomeDetail: The comment predicted near-zero musician uptake and no viable copyright path. Suno instead settled Warner Music's lawsuit in November 2025 and launched licensed models with WMG and BMG in September 2026, while the BBC reported around 100 million users.
entries.note: The stems/MIDI critique was technically fair. The conclusion that the product would remain a novelty was not.

entries.storyTitle: Gen-1: The Next Step Forward for Generative AI — Generating Videos
entries.outcome: Runway raised $308M at a $3B+ valuation and shipped Gen-4.

entries.author: tills13
entries.cardQuote: So aside from the integrations which do seem nice is their moat a good prompt or an I misunderstanding?
entries.quote: So aside from the integrations which do seem nice is their moat a good prompt or an I misunderstanding?
entries.outcome: Factory raised $200M at a $5B valuation and sold Droids to large enterprises.
entries.outcomeDetail: Factory's $50 million Series B valued it at $300 million in September 2025. By September 2026 it had raised $200 million at a $5 billion valuation, and Reuters reported the company was selling AI agents to enterprise engineering teams.
entries.note: The moat question was legitimate in a crowded agent market. The implied answer—that there was nothing beyond a prompt—was wrong.

entries.author: _lvbh
entries.cardQuote: I'm surprised there's still so much hype funding 3 years in. There's still no evidence LLMs lead to "superintelligence"
entries.quote: I'm surprised there's still so much hype funding 3 years in. There's still no evidence LLMs lead to "superintelligence" - it's interesting that's the word chosen by all these new startups
entries.storyTitle: Superintelligence startup Reflection AI launches with $130M in funding
entries.outcome: Reflection raised $2B at an $8B valuation seven months later.
entries.outcomeDetail: Reflection launched with $130 million at a $545 million valuation in March 2025. In October 2025 it raised $2 billion at an $8 billion valuation, a 15x jump, with Nvidia, Sequoia, Lightspeed, and Eric Schmidt participating.
entries.note: The skeptic was right that 'superintelligence' was doing a lot of work. He was wrong that investors were done funding the premise.

entries.author: simianparrot
entries.cardQuote: These generated videos are exactly the same nonsense as the spaghet videos, they've just got more data crammed in there. But nothing about them is consistent.
entries.quote: Doesn't mean it'll get any better though. Most technologies and algorithms have an end point. People thought flying cars were inevitable and imminent because after all, cars got so much better and feature-rich within a very short timespan. And then innovation practically stopped because there's a limit to possible energy storage and utilisation unless some magical new innovation comes along. But it hasn't. These generated videos are exactly the same nonsense as the spaghet videos, they've just got more data crammed in there. But nothing about them is consistent.
entries.outcomeDetail: Luma launched Dream Machine in June 2024. By November 2025 it had raised a $900 million Series C at a valuation above $4 billion, with HUMAIN, AMD Ventures, and Andreessen Horowitz participating.
entries.note: The 'AI video has plateaued' call was wrong. Luma's models improved through Ray2 and Ray3, and the category became a capital-intensive race rather than a dead end.
